segments.voice: Krishna is heading home to Dwaraka across a desert when he meets an old friend: the sage Uttanka, who has spent a long time in austerity and hasn't heard the news. Uttanka greets him warmly. So, did you make peace between the cousins? Krishna tells him the truth. There was no peace. The Kauravas are dead. And the sage's face changes. You could have stopped it, Uttanka says, and you didn't. He raises his hand to curse the man standing in front of him.
screen: `A SAGE IN THE DESERT.` → `"DID YOU MAKE PEACE?"` → `HE RAISES HIS HAND TO CURSE.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't flinch, and he doesn't argue first. Hear me out, he says, and then decide. He tells Uttanka he went to the Kauravas himself and they would not listen. Then, in the epic's telling, he shows Uttanka the same vast universal form Arjuna saw before the battle: the whole world inside God. The sage lowers his hand. Krishna offers him a gift, and Uttanka asks for something simple: water, whenever he needs it in this dry country. Think of me, Krishna says. Some time later Uttanka is wandering, desperately thirsty, and he remembers. Toward him comes a hunter, an outcast by the rules of the time, filthy, surrounded by dogs, offering water. Uttanka is disgusted and sends him away. Then Krishna appears. That was Indra, king of the gods, bringing you amrita, the drink of immortality, in that form, to see what you would do. Uttanka turned down immortality because of who was holding the cup. Here's the teaching. In the Gita, Krishna says the wise see the same in a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast. Hindus call it sama-darshana, equal vision: one divine Self living in every being. Uttanka had just seen God holding the whole world, and minutes later couldn't see God in one dusty man with dogs. Many teachers read the story as exactly that gap. Today the test rarely looks holy. It looks like the person you'd rather not take anything from.
screen: `"HEAR ME OUT FIRST"` · `THE UNIVERSAL FORM` · `AN OUTCAST HUNTER OFFERS A DRINK` · `IT WAS INDRA, CARRYING AMRITA` · then, large: `SAMA-DARSHANA: THE SAME GOD IN EVERY GIVER`

Picture them holding out something you need, notice honestly what rises in you, and bow to them silently, just a little. If you pray, hold them in your prayer, just as they are; if you don't, simply let the bow stand.

870.title: Parikshit and the act of truth
870.hook: Abhimanyu's son is born without breath, and the women of the house turn to Krishna

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Ashvamedhika, Uttanka refused water from an outcast hunter who turned out to be Indra, carrying amrita. Your line was sama-darshana: the wise see God in every giver.

segments.voice: After the night raid, Ashvatthama loosed a terrible weapon he couldn't call back, and turned it on the wombs of the Pandava women. Krishna answered him then with a promise: the child Uttara is carrying will live. Now the Pandavas are away in the mountains, fetching Marutta's gold. Uttara, Abhimanyu's young widow, goes into labor. The child is born, and he doesn't breathe. Kunti, Draupadi, Subhadra and Uttara herself are in that room. The promise is called in.
screen: `ASHVATTHAMA'S WEAPON.` → `KRISHNA'S PROMISE.` → `A CHILD BORN WITHOUT BREATH.`

segments.voice: The grief here is not quiet. Kunti, Abhimanyu's grandmother, reminds Krishna of his words: you promised this child would live. Subhadra, Krishna's own sister and Abhimanyu's mother, pleads with him. And Uttara speaks to the still baby in her arms, in Ganguli's telling, as if he could hear: your father died young, and now you have gone after him. Krishna goes into the birth room. He doesn't bargain or cast a weapon. He makes a declaration of truth. He names truths about his own life: that he has never spoken a falsehood, not even in jest, that he has never turned his back in battle, that righteousness is dear to him. By the force of those truths, he says, let this child live. The child stirs, and breathes. This boy is Parikshit, and the dynasty that was nearly erased goes on through him. Here's the teaching. Hindus call it satya, truth, and treat it as a real power. The Mundaka Upanishad says satyam eva jayate, truth alone wins; India carries those words under its national emblem. The epic shows what that means: a promise is only as strong as the life behind it. Krishna's word could hold a child because he hadn't spent his words carelessly, even in jest. Many teachers read the scene that way. Truthfulness isn't only not lying. It's a life whose words can be leaned on when it counts.
screen: `KUNTI: "YOU PROMISED"` · `UTTARA SPEAKS TO HER SON` · `A DECLARATION OF TRUTH` · `PARIKSHIT BREATHES` · then, large: `SATYAM EVA JAYATE: TRUTH ALONE WINS`

segments.voice: Many Hindus begin a puja with a sankalpa, a solemn intention spoken aloud, sometimes with a little water held in the right palm. Cup your right hand, and name, plainly, one promise you're still keeping, to a child, a friend, a parent, yourself. Then say one true sentence about how you try to live, one you could say out loud and mean, and open your hand. If you pray, offer that sentence in your prayer; if you don't, just let it be said.

segments.voice: The horse has been set loose at last. It wanders where it likes, and Arjuna follows with his bow, country after country, fighting the kings who challenge it. Then it walks into Manipura. Long ago, on his travels, Arjuna married a princess of this land, Chitrangada, and left a son here. That son, Babhruvahana, is king now. And he comes out of the city to meet the horse, not with an army but with gifts and brahmanas, his head bowed to his father.
screen: `THE HORSE WANDERS.` → `IT ENTERS MANIPURA.` → `HIS SON COMES OUT WITH GIFTS.`

segments.voice: Arjuna is angry. In Ganguli's telling he scolds his son: I've come as a warrior guarding a sacrificial horse, and you greet me like this? A king of your order should fight. Then someone rises out of the earth: Ulupi, the serpent princess, another of Arjuna's wives. Do what your father asks, she tells the young king. Fight him. So father and son meet in battle, and the son is very good. His arrow strikes Arjuna, and Arjuna falls and does not get up. Then Ulupi places a gem from the serpent world on Arjuna's chest, and he wakes as if from sleep. She explains: when Arjuna brought Bhishma down from behind Shikhandi, the Vasus, Bhishma's divine brothers, cursed him, and the curse was to end at his own son's hands. Today it did. Now the teaching underneath. Hindus call it svadharma, your own duty, and it changes with the role you're standing in. As a son, Babhruvahana bows. As the king whose land the horse has entered, he must ride out. Arjuna knows this from the inside. Before the war he begged not to fight his own grandfather and teacher, and Krishna told him in the Gita: better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than another's done well. Now the student of the Gita says it to his son. Many teachers read the scene as the Gita coming home, and the duty done fully is what frees Arjuna.
screen: `ARJUNA: "A KING SHOULD FIGHT"` · `THE SON'S ARROW FELLS THE FATHER` · `A GEM, AND AN OLD CURSE LIFTED` · `BOW AS SON, RIDE AS KING` · then, large: `SVADHARMA: THE DUTY OF YOUR ROLE`

segments.voice: Gold handed out to the brahmanas, food for everyone, kings and sages crowding the grounds: the horse is home, the sacrifice is done, and everyone says there's never been a rite like it. Then, from a hole in the ground, out comes a mongoose. One side of its body is gold. It looks around at all this splendor and speaks, in a voice like thunder: this sacrifice of yours isn't equal to a little barley flour given away by a poor brahmana in Kurukshetra. The crowd goes silent.
screen: `THE SACRIFICE IS DONE.` → `A MONGOOSE, HALF GOLD.` → `"NOT EQUAL TO A LITTLE FLOUR."`

segments.voice: In Kurukshetra, the mongoose explains, there lived a brahmana who fed his family by gleaning, picking up the grains left in the fields after harvest. A famine came, and the family went hungry for a long time. At last he gathered enough barley for a little flour, and they divided it four ways: the man, his wife, their son and the son's wife. Just as they were about to eat, a hungry guest arrived. The brahmana welcomed him and gave him his own share. The guest was still hungry. The wife gave hers. Then the son. Then the daughter-in-law. Then the guest revealed himself: he was Dharma, righteousness itself, and the family was carried to heaven. The mongoose had rolled in the scattered flour, and wherever it touched, its fur turned to gold. Half of it. Ever since, it has gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, hoping to turn the other half gold. It just rolled in Yudhishthira's. Nothing changed. Here's the teaching. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells a student going home: let your guest be a god to you, atithi devo bhava. That's why Hindu families feed the guest first, and in this story the guest really was Dharma. And in the Gita, Krishna asks only a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love. A gift is weighed by what it cost and the love in it, not by its size.

segments.voice: The news from Dwaraka reaches Hastinapura: Krishna is gone, and his clan has destroyed itself. Yudhishthira makes up his mind in one sentence, in Ganguli's telling: time is cooking all creatures. It's time to go. He crowns Parikshit, the child who was born without breath, now grown, and puts the kingdom in others' care. Then the five brothers and Draupadi take off their jewelry, put on the plain clothes of forest hermits, and walk out through the gates. The city follows a little way, weeping, and turns back. One companion does not turn back. A dog.

segments.voice: This is the Mahaprasthanika, the book of the great departure. The Pandavas walk east first: Yudhishthira leads, then Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Draupadi, and the dog behind them all. They reach the sea, and a figure stands in their path, tall as a mountain: Agni, the god of fire. He speaks to Arjuna. Remember the great bow Gandiva? Agni brought it to Arjuna long ago, from Varuna, lord of the waters. Its work is finished; it belongs to Varuna; give it back. And Arjuna, who carried it through the whole war, throws it into the waves and walks on unarmed. Here's the teaching. Hindu tradition maps a life in four stages: the student, the householder, then vanaprastha, the forest-dweller who hands the household on, and sannyasa, the renouncer who sets everything down. Many teachers read this morning as those last stages acted out: the kingdom to Parikshit, the jewels off at the gate, the bow back to the god it came from. The Isha Upanishad opens the same way: all this belongs to the Lord, so enjoy it by letting it go. That's why many Hindu elders still hand on jewelry, duties and the family puja, and set out on pilgrimage. Not as an ending. As the next stage. Then they walk on around the edge of the world, toward Meru. And the dog keeps coming.

segments.voice: Seven travelers climb into the Himalayas: five brothers, one queen, one dog. They cross the mountains and, beyond them, a great desert of sand, and far off they can see Meru, the mountain at the center of the world. They walk in single file, Yudhishthira in front, Draupadi near the back. Then, without warning, she drops to the ground. Bhima sees her fall. And the man at the front of the line keeps walking.
screen: `OVER THE MOUNTAINS.` → `A DESERT OF SAND, MERU AHEAD.` → `DRAUPADI FALLS.`

segments.voice: Bhima calls out to his elder brother. In Ganguli's telling, his question is simple: she never did anything wrong, so why has she fallen? Yudhishthira answers without stopping. She loved Arjuna more than the rest of us, he says. That is what she is paying for now. And he walks on, the text says, without looking at her. That's a hard sentence to sit with. Draupadi was dragged into the dice hall and humiliated. She lost her sons in the night raid. And at the end of the road, the reason given is that her heart leaned toward one husband. Hear the echo. In that dice hall, Draupadi asked the elders whether she had been lawfully staked, and Bhishma could only answer: the way of dharma is subtle. The tradition calls it sukshma dharma, subtle dharma. Right action is hard to see, even good people carry small faults, and the epic often refuses to close a hard case. So readers have argued about this verdict for centuries. Some hear the strict logic of the road. Some notice Yudhishthira never kneels, and ask what that costs him. And the tradition hasn't let her fall be the last word. The epic's final book shows Draupadi in heaven as Shri, the goddess of fortune, and in Tamil Nadu many villages worship her as Draupadi Amman. Arguing with the story is how Hindus keep it alive. The brothers walk on. The dog keeps walking.
screen: `BHIMA: "WHY HAS SHE FALLEN?"` · `A HARD SENTENCE TO SIT WITH` · `BHISHMA, IN THE DICE HALL: "DHARMA IS SUBTLE"` · `SUKSHMA DHARMA: ARGUE IT OUT` · then, large: `HER FALL IS NOT THE LAST WORD`

segments.voice: Sahadeva and Nakula are the youngest of the five, the twins, sons of Madri, raised by Kunti as her own. In this serial they have often stood just behind their older brothers: Sahadeva, known for his learning; Nakula, known as the handsome one. Now, on the road toward Meru, Sahadeva falls. A little later, Nakula falls too. Both times Bhima calls out to the front of the line, and both times Yudhishthira answers without stopping.
screen: `THE TWINS, SONS OF MADRI.` → `SAHADEVA FALLS.` → `THEN NAKULA.`

segments.voice: Listen to the shape of the answers. About Sahadeva, in Ganguli's telling: he thought no one was equal to him in wisdom. About Nakula: he thought no one was equal to him in beauty. The same sentence twice, with one word changed. Look at what isn't blamed. Not the learning. Not the good looks. Those are gifts, and the epic has praised both brothers for them. What trips each of them is a small private thought laid on top of the gift: no one is equal to me. Sahadeva's wisdom could have walked on with him. What he couldn't carry to the top of the world, in this telling, was the comparison. Here's the teaching. In the Gita, when Krishna lists what real knowledge looks like, the very first word is amanitva: humility, literally not thinking much of yourself. Sahadeva, the learned one, had the knowledge and missed the first item on the list. Notice he never said it out loud. Hindu teaching counts the private ranking too, the quiet no one is equal to me, because that's where pride lives first. Behind the line, the dog still walks. Three travelers are left with Yudhishthira now: Bhima, Arjuna and the dog. The road narrows as the people on it fall away.
screen: `"NONE EQUAL TO HIM IN WISDOM"` · `"NONE EQUAL TO HIM IN BEAUTY"` · `NOT THE GIFT, THE COMPARISON` · then, large: `AMANITVA: FIRST ON THE GITA'S LIST`
